items.title: Reed Mattison: Where the Grass Actually Is Greener
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Reed Mattison: Where the Grass Actually Is Greener

Born in Bowling Green, Kentucky, in 1997 and now living at the foot of the Tetons in Wyoming, American photographer Reed Mattison has published his first monograph with Origini Edizioni. The sequence measures what separates him from his home state and what keeps drawing him back.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Reed Mattison.

To and From opens on a painting of snow-capped mountains hanging in an abandoned trailer home. Mattison came across it while rummaging with his friend Louis through the trailer where Louis’s grandfather had lived, on the family farm in Somerset, in south-central Kentucky. He found the painting quite poignant. “Growing up in a rural place, especially in the South, the media and popular opinion tell us to go somewhere better,” he explains. “That the grass is always greener. I did move away to the majestic and wild Grand Tetons, but still I find myself back in Kentucky looking for myself, where the grass actually is greener.”

On one of his many trips home, a TSA agent at Nashville International Airport looked at his Wyoming ID: “Wyoming? You’re far from home.” “I knew what she meant,” the photographer recalls, “but I couldn’t help but think no, I was so close to home.” Trained in photojournalism, a discipline built on closing the gap, he nonetheless shoots his own people from behind, through foliage, out of focus. “A lot has changed since I’ve been gone and I feel left behind at times. Many of the photographs are distant and from behind because most of this project was catching up with my old home.”

Mattison long favored the intuitive quality of 35mm, then went looking for a change. For the scenes where people gather, he now brings out a 4×5 view camera. “The magnitude of the negative could capture the complexity of the place I was trying to photograph,” he notes. “Kentucky, like many places in the south, is slow. Our vowels, our meals, the seasons all crawl by, and that allowed me to take a slower approach and capture every blade of grass and bead of sweat.”

Nothing here belongs on a postcard. An obelisk surfaces above a cornfield: it marks, in Fairview, the birthplace of Jefferson Davis, president of the Confederate States during the Civil War. As a child, the photographer read it as the sign that his grandparents’ house was near. “I hate that guy and all he stood for,” he says. He also refuses to treat poverty as spectacle, as he believes reporters and big publications do when they travel south from the cities. “I was not poor and a lot of Kentuckians aren’t,” he insists. “It does plague our most vulnerable populations but will not be solved by exploiting them through photography. The poor and immigrant communities in Kentucky are fighting the good fight and have a powerful voice of their own. I wanted to photograph my experience because that is all I know.”

The book closes on a quotation from Wendell Berry, the poet and farmer who left New York to work his family’s land in Kentucky, taken from his 1970 essay Think Little. “No other author has explained how I feel about my home, the environment, and community like Berry,” Mattison says, and he hopes to follow him back one day: “There is still more juice in the fruit for me to squeeze.” He had long dreamed of publishing a book, unsure whether it would hold poems, a novel or photographs, yet certain he would dedicate it to someone he loved.

That someone is Clay, his brother, whom he hated for years, to the point of violence. “There is a parallel between my relationship with Clay and my relationship with being born in the South,” he observes. “We were taught to be ashamed of ourselves and that the South was bad.” 

The two men grew close as the photographer came to see how diverse and progressive his home state had always been. “He forgave me for all I’d done. He is my best friend. I want to make him proud and I hope he is proud of me.”

No one chooses a brother, or a birthplace. Reed Mattison has chosen both.

 

 

To and From by Reed Mattison, Origini Edizioni, handmade binding, €75.

items.title: Julie Glassberg, Life in Full Neon
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Julie Glassberg, Life in Full Neon

The French photographer has taken over the Carré de Baudouin, in Paris’s 20th arrondissement, with “L’être et le néon” , an immersive exhibition devoted to three communities who, from Sunday dance halls to Japanese highways, inject color into the everyday.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Julie Glassberg.

Some gestures slip past the usual categories of work and leisure. Painting a truck in flames, dancing every Sunday despite the passing years, building bicycles made for vertiginous jousts: so many ways of reclaiming one’s body, one’s turf, one’s life.

One day, on the terrace of La Coupole, the storied brasserie on Boulevard du Montparnasse (Paris’s 14th arrondissement), an elegant older woman told the photographer she came to dance every Sunday, sometimes finding love along the way. That encounter gave rise to Stayin’ Alive, winner of the BnF’s Grande Commande in 2022: portraits of seniors for whom retirement is no obstacle to staying active, or to having fun.

In New York, Julie Glassberg joined the Black Label Bike Club, founded in 1992 in Minneapolis, pioneers of tall-bikes and anarchic jousting. That immersion produced Bike Kill, a portrait of a punk, grunge, and hippie community resisting consumer culture and cultivating human connection.

In Japan, Julie Glassberg spent eight years documenting the life of the Utamarokai club and crossed paths with Tajima-san, owner of the truck Ichibanboshi. Born as an advertising gimmick, these neon-drenched cabs tell, beneath their bad-boy image, stories of nostalgia and childhood dreams made real. Never exhibited before, the Dekotora series, subject of a forthcoming book from Patrick Frey this year, closes out this vivid, color-soaked triptych.




“L’être et le néon” is on view through October 3rd, 2026, at the Carré de Baudouin in Paris. Note: the venue closes for its summer break from August 10 to 24, 2026, inclusive.

items.title: From the Camargue to Patagonia, Axelle de Russé and Théo Giacometti Hold the Line
items.content:
IN IMAGES

From the Camargue to Patagonia, Axelle de Russé and Théo Giacometti Hold the Line

An ocean divides them, yet Axelle de Russé and Théo Giacometti are photographing two embattled territories, both threatened by rising waters.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Axelle de Russé & Théo Giacometti.

Icebound Patagonia and the salt-flats of the Camargue share neither climate nor language. And yet Axelle de Russé and Théo Giacometti are tracking down a common essence in both places: that of edgelands, landscapes worked over by wind and salt, by myth, and by the diffuse sense of a vanishing yet to come. Their images refuse the dry statement of documentary in favor of drift, of suspension, that murky zone where the real and the dreamed sometimes bleed into one another.

Drawn to little-documented territories, Axelle de Russé works within the tradition of the photographer-explorer. Since 2016 she has been photographing Puerto Williams, in Chilean Patagonia, billed as the southernmost city on earth, in a kind of echo of Longyearbyen in the Norwegian Arctic. Infrared film tints the trees a muted red there, drawing the planet’s two opposite poles visually closer together.

“When the salt has stiffened our hair and our hands,” writes Théo Giacometti of Axelle de Russé’s images, “when the sailors’ songs hold no more secrets for us, then we can let ourselves slip under, sink into the hallucinated landscapes of her Patagonia, a ghost-land she rouses with her love and delivers back to us complete with its exiles, its myths, and this way of declaring: we are still here.”

 

In his portraits of gauchos and exiles, Théo Giacometti, a regular contributor to the press, unfolds the full range of a personal artistic practice attentive to the ties between landscape, memory, narrative, and human presence. In the Camargue, he has been building Pour qui chanteront les sirènes (For Whom the Sirens Will Sing), a story born of an artificial land woven together from dikes between the Rhône and the Mediterranean. Medium-format film imposes its own grain, its silences, its slowness.

“You plunge into Théo Giacometti’s images as into deep water,” says Axelle de Russé, comparing his Camargue portraits to hers. “I see the same faces, the same expressions of those who are viscerally bound to a territory, who have become one with it, their fates tied together in sorrow. These are lands one does not leave, ‘for better or for worse.'”

The two artists had read each other’s work before exhibiting together. To describe the wind that batters Navarino Island, Théo Giacometti calls on the Chilean writer Francisco Coloane. Facing a Camargue horseman, Axelle de Russé finds again the faces of Puerto Williams. The same set of the mouth crosses both hemispheres, the same rootedness in a territory that the women and men they photograph inhabit with their whole being, body and soul alike.

Neither yields to dread: from Patagonia to the Camargue, beauty is a choice. A way of protecting what one loves by showing it as desirable rather than as already lost. Their two worlds converged in Paris, at La Maison des Photographes, for an exhibition in June 2026 titled “Et après, la mer” (“And After, the Sea”). The water keeps advancing, and they will keep documenting these last strongholds of resistance at the crumbling edge of a world.

 

Axelle de Russé: axellederusse.com

Théo Giacometti: theogiacometti.com

items.title: Walter Chandoha Herds Cats
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Walter Chandoha Herds Cats

Ahead of International Cat Day on 8 August, we look back at Family Cats from the Archive 1949-1962, recently published by Damiani. A largely unpublished collection from the man widely considered the father of modern cat photography.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Walter Chandoha.

“Cats! They drive you crazy and they blind you with love,” writes Grace Coddington, former creative director of Vogue US, at the opening of the book’s foreword. In 1949, as a snowstorm sweeps New York, Walter Chandoha, a young freelance photographer just demobilised after serving in the US Signal Corps, picks up a stray kitten and slips it into his coat pocket to give to his wife, Maria. Each evening, between 11 p.m. and 11:10 p.m., the kitten gives in to fits of madness that Chandoha starts to capture on film. He names him Loco, Spanish for “mad.”

“I smile every time I see his little clown kitten laughing at the camera. Or Loco boxing himself in front of the mirror, like a real pro,” Grace Coddington confides. Those images charm the illustrated press worldwide: Life, National Geographic, greeting cards, calendars and puzzles soon carry his likeness.

Those pictures would shape the rest of his career. Walter Chandoha went on portraying cats until the age of 98, across some thirty books, and suspected Andy Warhol of borrowing from his work for certain illustrations in 25 Cats Name Sam and One Blue Pussy, privately printed in 1957.

Beyond the cats themselves, the archive documents domestic New York in the 1950s. Family apartments in Queens, neighborhood streets long since vanished, a studio set up inside the family house, where Maria helped prepare and settle the models.

Every cat that sat for him came from adoption, many through Greenwich Village’s Humane League. Together they form a distillation of tenderness, to be discovered one by one. As Grace Coddington puts it: “Seen through Walter’s lens you feel each cat personality beaming out, an endless supply of leaping, bounding, yawning kittens at his disposal.”


Walter Chandoha, Family Cats from the Archive 1949-1962, foreword and illustration by Grace Coddington, Damiani, €18.

items.title: Fifty Years Ago, Joel Meyerowitz Tipped Into the Light
items.content:
White cottages lined up along a road. A telephone booth lit against the dusk. A Ford station wagon parked beside the ocean. Laundry that the wind fills like sails. These pictures carry a taste of nostalgia, of seaside holidays, of vintage color, of a certain carelessness.

In 1976, Joel Meyerowitz is thirty-eight. For nearly fifteen years he has photographed the streets of New York in small format, at a thousandth of a second, in the vicinity of Garry Winogrand and Lee Friedlander. He already teaches color at Cooper Union. That year he receives a grant from the New York State Council on the Arts and buys a view camera.

“I made a leap in the dark,” he writes in the new preface that opens this edition, “or as it turned out, a leap into the light.” He measures the cost of the gesture today. “For a Bronx-born street photographer, giving up the jazz-inflected rhythms and spontaneity of city life for an 8-by-10-inch view camera and the shadow-free luminosity of the outer Cape was a welcome, and subsequently life-changing, challenge.”

His camera, a Deardorff that left the workshop in 1938, the year of the photographer’s birth, repays attention. Meyerowitz admires its “shining mahogany face” and notes that the brass and leather carry the record of past outings “like the medals and decorations on the chest of an old veteran.”

The whole outfit weighs some forty-five pounds, to be carried across sand. A wide-field Ektar lens of 250 millimeters takes in slightly less than ordinary human vision. The film, a Vericolor II Type L rated at 80 ASA, was balanced for tungsten and called for a filter in daylight. Meyerowitz went without, correcting the color at the printing stage instead.

By day the exposure ran half a second at f/90, an aperture so narrow that everything holds sharp, from the foreground to the horizon. At the end of the day it stretched from four to ten minutes. “It’s not a film for horse races,” Meyerowitz remarks with amusement in the technical note that closes the book.

“For the first time in my life I slowed down, took a deep breath, and watched the slow, incremental movements of light and shadow cross a sandbar in the ebbing tide,” the photographer recalls, his eye fixed on “sunlight raking over clapboard siding.” He thinks of Edward Hopper, who painted these same shores for many years.

Out of that slow fever come discoveries about photography, and about himself. “How strange it was to find myself softening, and entering into moments of communion with such numinous and evanescent things.” The image forms on a ground glass, where the photographer composes it. Meyerowitz found a doorway there: everything held “the potential for new meaning, especially when seen upside down under the dark cloth of the view camera.”

Cape Light appeared in 1978 from New York Graphic Society, with an interview by Bruce K. MacDonald, then dean of the School of the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, which exhibited the series that same year. By 2016, sales had already passed one hundred and fifty thousand copies.

Aperture published its first edition of the book in 2015. For this fiftieth anniversary, the images have been entirely remastered once again, after several months of work and scans that read the negative point by point, drawing out shades of color the processes of the day could not render. Meyerowitz welcomes the result: “The images printed here have come back with a fidelity to the original moment of which no previous edition had been capable.”

Here again is the door opening onto the Atlantic in Doorway to the Sea, Provincetown, the cream corridor of Hartwig House, Truro, the red interior of Red Interior, Provincetown beneath a hazy moon. Forty images with which Meyerowitz, alongside William Eggleston and Stephen Shore, pulled color out of the commercial purgatory where the art world still kept it confined.

Joel Meyerowitz: Cape Light (50th Anniversary Edition), photographs and preface by Joel Meyerowitz, is published by Aperture, 112 pages, 40 images. £45
items.excerpt: Aperture reissues Cape Light, the cult book that brought color into the museum. Its author, now eighty-eight, recounts the sojourn on Cape Cod spent in “a meditative state of grace.”

items.title: They Shoot Dingoes, Don’t They?
items.content:
Picture the scene: no sheep to be found, no farm to protect, nothing but a stretch of arid Australian bush. And there, on the edge of the track, strung up by the neck from a sign, the desiccated carcass of a dingo, “hung out as a trophy.” This deeply unsettling photograph closes Ten Eighty, published by Tall Poppy Press, the imprint Matt Dunne has run since 2021.

Trained as a teacher, with a background in history before photography, Matt Dunne now runs photobook-making workshops. His work explores ecology, colonialism and mythology through the country and seeks to make the widespread war on the animal visible: first the wedge-tailed eagle, whose slaughter he traced in The Killing Sink, published in 2022, now the dingo.

Since the arrival of white settlers, the publisher notes, the dingo has been one of the most persecuted animals in Australia, targeted by shooting, trapping and poison alike. Federal law nonetheless classifies it as a native species, on a par with the kangaroo and the koala and the other species present in Australia before the sixteenth century. Why, the photographer asks, do we still treat as a pest an animal essential to the balance of the ecosystem?

The book’s opening pages unspool photograph after photograph of the Dog Fence: over 5,500 kilometres of wire fencing running from the South Australian coast to Queensland, a distance longer than that between Los Angeles and New York, or between Paris and Moscow. North of the line, where cattle graze largely unbothered by the dingo, the animal is at home; south of it, where the first flocks of sheep arrived with colonisation, that same animal, rebranded a “wild dog” by the authorities, is an outlaw.

“We find, in this fence, not just a physical barrier, not just an environmental barrier, but a convenient division for what is legal and what is not,” Matt Dunne writes. This category of “wild dog” serves precisely to sidestep the animal’s federal status. “The term ‘wild dogs’ is a euphemism,” he notes, “with dingoes being the only actual wild dogs in Australia.”

“Sheep farming advocacy groups, policy documents, hunters and poison manufacturers continue to use the phrase ‘wild dog’ to mislead the public, masking that a native animal is what’s being targeted,” the photographer continues, and his book is built against the grain of that hazy language. He borrows from critic Colin Pantall the notion of the exploded view, the technical diagram that shows an object’s parts pulled apart.

Alongside Matt Dunne’s photographs sit a painting by George Stubbs from 1772, images of hunts held in full costume in the 1830s, and receipts issued to Aboriginal stockmen in exchange for dingo pelts. The book’s title, Ten Eighty, names the lethal, antidote-less poison used to wipe the animal out: 1080, sodium fluoroacetate, banned across most of the world.

In Australia, it is dropped from the air over pastoral land and loaded into capsule baits that burst the instant the animal bites down. Matt Dunne photographs the arsenal with the coolness of an inventory: a five-litre blue jerrycan, white buckets stacked under a brand called De-K9, a bottle of strychnine labelled by a manufacturer in Saint-Ouen, France.


To Australia’s First Nations, the author reminds us, the animal is sacred. Their national declaration, an excerpt of which he reproduces, leaves no room for doubt: “Killing Dingoes is killing family.” Himself descended from a line of settlers, Matt Dunne unsettles his own people’s conscience from that very position. The book closes on the question that the sight of that dingo, strung up on the wire, leaves him asking: “Is this really the best we can do?”

Ten Eighty by Matt Dunne is published by Tall Poppy Press, 2026.
items.excerpt: In Ten Eighty, Australian photographer Matt Dunne documents the fate of the dingo, a native animal that First Nations peoples hold sacred and that the descendants of settlers are intent on eradicating.

items.title: Daniel Dorsa Shoots Greenland’s Youth
items.content:
The idea sparked on Instagram. In 2022, a high school friend of the photographer’s, now a microbiologist, posted images from Greenland, where she was tracking how microbes in glacial meltwater change from source to ocean. Her research team takes its name, S.I.L.A., from the Inuit concept of sila, which denotes both the physical world and a spiritual way of living within it.

Daniel Dorsa pitched the story to the American press, was turned down, and went anyway. “Greenland is often seen in the United States and much of the western world as a desolate expanse of ice,” he writes. “This project challenges that notion.” His landing in Kangerlussuaq, in the spring of 2023, could almost have proven him wrong.

“Snow and strong winds from the north pelt the plane as it lands on the cold war era tarmac, twenty-five kilometers from the ice sheet,” he notes. The scientists’ work resists him, offering little to photograph. Worn down by years of assignments, the photographer falls back on an old instinct, inherited from skateboarding: let the place dictate the looking, with no plan set in advance.


The country’s raw whiteness strikes him first. “White is not actually a color, but the encapsulation of all the visible wavelengths of light,” he writes. His lens then turns to the wooden houses painted blue, red, and yellow, which cut against the snow with a graphic boldness. Then come the faces, alongside the human connections he forges. And the book turns a corner.

A young woman with turquoise dreadlocks tilts her chin toward the sky, a fly inked beneath her jaw, three words tattooed across her throat: Master of Disaster. This is far from the familiar image of the Inuit. Other scenes extend the same gaze. Four young men in sneakers pose with beers in hand and cigarettes between their lips, in front of a construction site. Two shirtless teenagers, in full summer sun, balance on one another in an acrobatic pose.

Elsewhere, a young woman lies in the grass in Nuuk, white sneakers on her feet, wearing a dreamy expression. On graduation day, students in embroidered vests and white caps dance in a circle, arm in arm. Daniel Dorsa looks at this youth without condescension. “This place hardens you, after all. You grow up quick when nothing is guaranteed to you. The only things you can rely on are the elements,” he writes in the text accompanying the book.

Among the encounters that stand out, Nava holds a place apart. The young woman runs a hostel in Sisimiut with her stepmother. Openly queer, born into a family of dog sledders, she takes the photographer out on a snowmobile in -22°F weather. “As we rode through the mountains, nearly invisible bumps in the snow bounced me around like a drunk cowboy on a mechanical bull,” he recounts.


That evening, the young woman asks him to photograph her in her traditional furs. Daniel Dorsa, who is normally wary of images that exoticize their subject, agrees anyway, and counts this portrait among his favorites in the book. Nava’s pride, standing in her sealskin, disarms the cliché with its soft tones.

Color, elsewhere in the book, follows an inverse logic: bright primaries clash against the white, while somber duotones, emptied of people, interrupt the tumult like rests in a musical score. The object itself extends this logic of contrast. The silkscreened cover disappears beneath a translucent vellum jacket, on which Clint Woodside, founder of Deadbeat Club, had excerpts from Daniel Dorsa’s journal printed: the text overlays the image before the book is even opened.

Because politics has a way of intruding where least expected, that winter the American president, Donald Trump, reaffirmed his intention to annex Greenland, by force if necessary. Daniel Dorsa wonders whether that is why twelve-year-old Miki refuses to have his portrait taken, before putting himself in the boy’s place: “I can’t blame him if so. I’d probably think I was a spy too.”

A few days later, in Nuuk, his friend Inuuteq drives past the city’s maximum security prison. Does the word freedom, as the West understands it, even mean anything in the Arctic? “Americans are the only people in the world that love to talk about freedom,” he states. “But, the only people I’ve ever heard speak about freedom are prisoners.”

To Skip a Sinking Stone by Daniel Dorsa is published by Deadbeat Club Press and available for pre-order for $65.
items.excerpt: Setting out to document the work of glaciologists, the Los Angeles–based American photographer ended up training his lens on the snow, the architecture, and then the tattooed, pierced youth of Nuuk and Sisimiut.

items.title: Ugandan Women Carry Everything on Their Heads, and the Country’s Future on Their Shoulders
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Ugandan Women Carry Everything on Their Heads, and the Country's Future on Their Shoulders

With HeadStrong. The Women of Rural Uganda, New Yorker Dan Nelken and Ugandan writer Beatrice Lamwaka celebrate the working women who, at the quarry and in the marketplace alike, hold up a society scarred by war and governed by a patriarchal order.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Dan Nelken & Adele Quartley Brown.

To photograph these women, Dan Nelken set up a portable studio at the roadside, in the middle of the market, at the entrance to the quarry, and hung behind them, whenever circumstances allowed, a length of mosquito netting that veils the setting without erasing it, letting a market stall, a heap of rubble, the outline of a mango tree show through.

The photographer claims kinship with the Northern European portraitists of the 17th and 18th centuries and with Face of Our Time, the collection of faces published by the German photographer August Sander in 1929. From them he takes the direct address to the viewer and the tool of the trade held firmly in hand, each woman presenting herself as she wishes to be seen, with the implement that best embodies her skill.

For more than twenty years, the Lord’s Resistance Army, a guerrilla movement claiming Christian inspiration and led by Joseph Kony, fought Yoweri Museveni’s government in the north of the country, abducting children from the villages to swell its ranks. Medical anthropologist Stella Nyanzi, who wrote the book’s foreword, notes that forced marriage is often the only way out for orphaned girls taken in by relatives with nothing to spare.

Aciro Vicky, 18, carries her son Michael tied to her back in a blue cloth, a jerrycan of gravel balanced on her hip and a hammer in her fist. Orphaned as a small child, raised by her maternal aunt, married at 15, she wanted to become a doctor. Of her parents she says only: “I don’t even remember their faces.”

Aloyo Nancy, 32, sells groundnut paste with Angel, 12 months, balanced on her hip. Apur Janet, 38, has been breaking stone for 10 years and feeds her eight children alone since her husband’s amputation. Acayo Margaret, 59, a retired nurse, has opened a village clinic and pays school fees for 10 children. Afiya Namazzi, 29, designs audio video games for the visually impaired.

The book draws its strength from this writing in two voices. The 66 portraits are answered by 36 accounts gathered by Beatrice Lamwaka, president of PEN Uganda, who kept following her interviewees through the two years the borders stayed closed. Stone breakers, a mechanic, a midwife, a motorcycle taxi driver, a video game designer: each portrait comes with a name, an age and a trade, and restores the sovereignty of women whom poverty has not deprived of power.




HeadStrong. The Women of Rural Uganda by Dan Nelken is published by Kehrer Verlag and is available for €45.

items.title: Miami Reframed
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Miami Reframed

With Miami in Color, photographer Marianne Doz pares the city down to its planes, angles, and light.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Marianne Doz.

Marianne Doz frames only walls. She cuts the sidewalk, the passerby, and the sign, everything that would date the scene, keeping only the wall, its edge, and the shadow that crosses it. This taste for bare form comes, no doubt, from sculpture, which has captivated her since childhood as much as photography has.

The turn came in 2014, on the Isle of Skye in Scotland, during a trip guided by professional photographers who introduced her to what she calls “true photography.” Grounded by lockdown, she turned her lens on the buildings of her Paris neighborhood, before carrying the method to Miami. The book moves through four neighborhoods: Miami Beach, Wynwood, Downtown, and the Design District, where she captures a palm frond’s shadow laid across pink and a red spiral staircase set within an opening edged in yellow.

Around 1980, in South Beach, designer Leonard Horowitz, co-founder of the Miami Design Preservation League, devised for the district’s fading Art Deco buildings a palette of pastels drawn, he said, from sunrises and sunsets, from the ocean, and from the sand. The district, repainted over the course of the decade, became the backdrop for the police drama Miami Vice. The show gave the genre its linen blazer and its bare ankles, the signature look of actor Don Johnson.

Every photograph passes through post-production. There Marianne Doz chooses one color, or a pairing of two, and backs it into a corner. The painter Josef Albers, who taught at the Bauhaus and later at Yale, showed in his book Interaction of Color that a color changes appearance according to whatever borders it. By leaving only two or three planes of color in the frame, Marianne Doz lets the blue of the sky set the temperature of whatever pink or orange it touches.

Among the images, one page, entirely red, carries a line from the German-American architect Mies van der Rohe: “Architecture begins when you place two bricks carefully together.” The red of that page belongs to the book’s palette, so the quotation becomes a color plate in its own right. Marianne Doz turns the architect on his head: she takes the structure apart and keeps only the paint that covered it. In her world, walls stand by color alone, without the bricks.




Miami in Color by Marianne Doz, published by Trope Publishing Co., is available for pre-order at the price of $30.

items.title: Theo Zeal: a Friend as Compass, a Wasteland as Eden
items.content:
“I followed Adam as he foraged on the Isle of Mull. Elsewhere, I looked for people in places where there were none, and kept returning. I placed Adam into this landscape and he made it his own.” These three sentences are the only ones in the book: no sequence titles, no captions, no dates. Nothing to interfere between the photographs and this reading pact.

Theo Zeal studied literature and philosophy in London before turning to photography. While making a short documentary about mudlarks, those scavengers of the Thames mud, he realised it was the still frame that interested him, more than the moving narrative. He is self-taught, through books and YouTube.

A book by American photographer John Gossage, whose own books are works in their own right, conceived with an extreme attention to sequencing and layout, reveals to him the total freedom a photographer has over a sequence. He begins to roam the estuary, east of London, parcels of land with no factories, no houses.

Lyme disease catches up with him during these expeditions: confusion, exhaustion, a feeling of floating outside his own head. British doctors have nothing to offer against symptoms they struggle to manage. Left to his own devices, the photographer goes to visit his oldest friend, Adam, living on Mull, in the Inner Hebrides.

On this wild, sparse island, Adam forages for roots and herbs to flavour his vodka. Theo Zeal follows him without asking anything of him, searching for “how to photograph the feeling of no longer feeling like yourself,” as he later told the Small Photobook Cult podcast. Walking behind someone becomes a method of orientation.

The breakthrough comes by accident, the day the prints from both series, the photographs from Mull and those from the estuary, end up side by side. Adam appears to be foraging amid rubble. This slippage of island into wasteland will become the architecture of the book, whose layout received particular care.

Graphic designer Martina Soffritti tightened the format of the cardboard A4 that Theo Zeal printed at home, alternated paper types from one sequence to the next, produced the cover in a yellow and midnight blue duotone, left the Swiss binding exposed and the spine blank. The volume looks found rather than published, as perishable as a forgotten print.

Adam almost never appears face-on, but from behind, off-centre, or swallowed by the edge of the frame. He is sometimes reduced to a leg, or two hands closed around sea pinks, those small rose-coloured coastal flowers. “I wanted him to look dwarfed by the nature around him,” Theo Zeal tells the same podcast.

A rare frontal image catches him bare-chested, kneeling among flowers, head down. The only digital shot in the book, taken with a borrowed camera after his Pentax 67 broke, shows him tiny at the back of a wood. Remove him from the frame: no scale remains, no landmark, no way out.

The landscape has deliberately been stripped of all geographical markers. “I wanted to create a world where only Adam existed.” One cannot tell whether one is on an island, on the edge of a suburb, or beneath a motorway flyover. Theo Zeal captures involuntary still lifes: a pile of bricks, a white sheet among the grass.

The rest happens in the darkroom. He develops his negatives in caffenol, a mixture of instant coffee and washing soda crystals, ruins many of them, then prints the survivors onto out-of-date paper bought cheaply. This pursuit of chemical accident places him in the lineage of two photographers who made it a method.

First, the British Stephen Gill, who buried his prints in the soil of Hackney Wick so that the place itself might finish the image. Then the American Sally Mann, who keeps on her collodion plates the dust and streaks that others wipe away. Each print becomes a rescue operation: salvaging a legible image from what he has himself damaged.

In keeping with his work, the author’s acknowledgements are of total economy. A single line: “Thank you to Adam for his friendship.” That is also the entire subject.

Adam by Theo Zeal is published by L’Artiere, 84 pages, €45.
items.excerpt: The British photographer spent four years following his childhood friend across a Hebridean island, before slipping those images between photographs of wasteland along the Thames estuary. In the book, Adam appears to be foraging for herbs amid the rubble.

items.title: Steve Schapiro’s Jazz Years: Before Baldwin, Before the Movement
items.content:
Among my collections photography books in my New York City apartment, one of my treasures is a large format limited edition of James Baldwin’s The Fire Next Time with photographs by Steve Schapiro that was published in 2017. Schapiro had followed Baldwin for LIFE magazine, and his work documenting the Civil Rights Movement was published widely and is in numerous museum collections.

Schapiro’s photographs of Baldwin and the Civil Rights Movement have always struck me. He wasn’t the only photographer doing this work, but his photographs have a certain humanity to them. His gaze and his closeness to the subjects makes his photographs unmistakably his.

But before his career as a photojournalist with LIFE, Time, Sports Illustrated and other major publications took off, Shapiro was a young freelance photographer who snagged a gig with Riverside Records, and he began photographing jazz shows, musicians, venues, recording sessions, and gatherings both in New York and Chicago.

According to jazz journalist Richard Scheinin, who wrote the text for the book, Schapiro’s interest in jazz began around 1960 or 1961, when he was hanging out in the loft of photographer W. Eugene Smith in the wholesale flower district of Manhattan, which had become a haunt for jazz musicians. 

“Maybe Schapiro was just struck by how interesting these musicians were as people,” Scheinin says. “Whatever it was, his interest was piqued and he wound up blanketing the jazz scene: downtown at the Village Vanguard in Greenwich Village, midtown at Riverside’s recording studio in Rockefeller Center, and uptown at the Apollo Theater in Harlem where he shot beautiful intimate photos of Sonny Rollins, Nina Simone, and many others including Aretha Franklin who was 19 years old and performing as part of Count Basie’s revue.”

And he continued to photograph jazz right up till the time of his first big assignment photographing Baldwin traveling in the Jim Crow era South, which started in early 1963. The book includes photographs from late 1962, when he photographed Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers during a recording session for their album Caravan.

It is also not hard to see in this “early” work what also makes his Civil Rights photographs stand out. The intimacy and warmth is there. The closeness and caring are there. And there is more to the connection between the two bodies of work than just Schapiro’s eye. 

“Part of the connection has to do with his unique ability to capture those hidden moments. But also, Schapiro was always interested in social justice; it was a theme in his photos right up until the end of his life when he took photos at Black Lives Matter demonstrations,” Scheinin wrote. “My guess is that in the early ‘60s, Schapiro understood that jazz was connected to the fight for civil rights. The music conveyed urgency and passion. It expressed the energy of the times. It was in many ways a soundtrack for the Civil Rights Movement.”

With the publication of the book Jazz: Best of the Apollo, Village Vanguard, and Riverside Sessions, Schapiro’s remarkable career adds another chapter, one that more fully shows the power of his photography and finally sheds light on work that has not been seen in decades.

Jazz: Best of the Apollo, Village Vanguard, and Riverside Sessions is published by ACC Art Books, and is available for $75.

items.title: The Egg Before the Hen, the Photograph Before History
items.content:
In 1923, in a Paris studio, a man in a dark suit stares intently at an egg balanced in an egg cup, as if waiting for it to confess. This photograph opens “Premières fois / Premières photos” (“First Times / First Photographs”), the exhibition Luce Lebart has curated for the Pavillon Populaire in Montpellier (France), running through November 1, to mark the Bicentennial of photography. Two hundred years of mislaid patents, tiny beginnings and founding gestures, told room by room by the woman who gathered them.

That egg belongs to a device called a mirœuf, a curious household appliance from 1923, unveiled the following year at the Salon des appareils ménagers, which judges the freshness of a shell through a slightly tilted mirror, on a principle close to that of the camera itself. A little further along in the same preamble sit sealed envelopes, deposited by inventors with the academies of science to protect their secrets. They are opened, Luce Lebart notes, only in the event of a priority dispute, as happened with Louis Ducos du Hauron’s patent for the invention of color. The rest remain sealed, silent guardians of an inventive 19th century.

Playful, but never idle: the word “firsts” itself took time to settle. Luce Lebart had first imagined something more technical, more serious, before realizing the chosen term would be more poetic, capable of humor too. “This isn’t an exhibition just for specialists”, she recalls. “Here, we’re popular. For me, it’s really important to be accessible to everyone. Otherwise, it doesn’t interest me.” The wall texts, deliberately short, are written “for people in a hurry”.

The same spirit runs through the neighboring corridor, where clusters of crystals catch the eye: the snowflakes of Wilson Bentley, an amateur meteorologist from Vermont who, from adolescence, attached a camera to his microscope and devoted his entire life to the pursuit. More than four thousand snowflakes photographed, each one different. “Every crystal is unique, they are all firsts”, sums up the exhibition’s curator, turning that plain fact into a method for the whole show.

Oblivion as part of invention

This playful stance doesn’t rule out political ones. The exhibition proper opens with a woman, and the choice is no accident. “For me, it was obviously interesting, important, and political to open a photography exhibition not with pioneers, but with a pioneer,” Luce Lebart explains. Anna Atkins, an English botanist trained in photography by her father, published between 1843 and 1853 the first book illustrated with photography, Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions. She signed her plates with the initials A. A., long read as those of an “Anonymous Amateur,” before her name was restored to her.

This pioneer opens the way to a gallery of far more anonymous figures. Next comes the constellation of patents, 4,000 filed in the 19th century and held in the archives of the Institut national de la propriété industrielle (National Institute of Industrial Property), 4,000 inventors of photography of whom, more often than not, only a name on a form remains. The “point Nadar,” a mark accompanying his patent for aerial photography, is still used today in aerial survey work. The devices designed to hold bodies still in studio settings explain, in hindsight, the stiffness of period portraits. One camera stand doubles as a bicycle kickstand, much to the amusement of Montpellier’s city hall, in a city where people cycle freely.

From the inventors’ anonymity to the trademarks’ fame is often just one patent away. The trademark filings tell another story, that of the shift from laboratory experiment to factory product. “These trademarks really show photography’s shift from an experimental object to a factory product”, notes Luce Lebart. Kodak, a rootless word chosen by George Eastman for its pronounceability in every language, embodies on its own the birth of branding.

Oblivion, however, can also strike the victors. Two Niépce daguerreotypes face each other across the same wall, one preserved, the other engraved by Niépce’s own hand in tribute to Daguerre: “My dear devoted friend Daguerre”. The View from the Window at Le Gras, taken in 1826 and held in Austin, Texas, was only identified as the first photograph in the early 1950s, when collectors rediscovered it. Before that, another image, now lost, held that role, including in Roland Barthes’s Camera Lucida. “It’s a bit like the Loch Ness monster, cryptozoology,” Luce Lebart jokes. A war memorial in Chalon still bears, because of this confusion, the mistaken date of 1822. The centenary was celebrated in 1924, the 150th anniversary in 1989. In 2026, both dates are marked at once.

Against this belated glory, the other side of the story: Hippolyte Bayard, inventor of a rival process, staged his own Self-Portrait as a Drowned Man in 1840, having received neither the recognition nor the pension granted to Daguerre and Niépce’s heir. His images, never fixed, fade in the light before reviving in darkness, as if the process replayed, each time, the oblivion its inventor suffered.

Seeing far, seeing fast

After oblivion, brilliance. Color fills an entire room: the experiments of Louis Ducos du Hauron, the Lumière brothers’ first Autochromes, and the 68,000 Autochromes of the Archives de la Planète (Archives of the Planet) gathered by Albert Kahn, among them the first color photographs of Algeria, including a stereoscopic anaglyph image of a Berber woman, long wrongly credited to an American invention.

A full chapter is devoted to long-distance transmission. During the Siege of Paris in 1871, René Dagron microfilmed messages to send them by carrier pigeon between Paris and Bordeaux. Arthur Batut, for his part, wrote a treatise on kite photography. Nadar backdated his patent for aerial photography, actually taken in 1868, after an American had beaten him to it. Édouard Belin transmitted the first landscape, the first portrait by wire, and in 1931 Pope Pius XI himself posed before the bélinographe to be transmitted by wireless, the Church having, since the Annunciation, always followed questions of long-distance communication closely.

The same vertigo of capturing things from afar runs through the room devoted to clouds, which can be neither bottled nor stuffed. Perhaps that is why meteorologists, unable to study the cloud itself, became photographers of clouds, giving rise to the first international cloud atlas, whose current edition still derives directly from it. Luce Lebart is devoting her next book to the subject, out in the coming days.

Luce Lebart has also unearthed, in Montpellier’s municipal archives, the city’s oldest photographs of skateboarding. Further on, Étienne-Jules Marey’s famous cat, caught at the exact moment it turns in midair, is a reminder that chronophotography fed medical research just as much as sports photography.

After the inventors and the technical feats, the final stretch of the show changes register: the photographers themselves get to speak. A photograph by Henri Cartier-Bresson, taken in 1922 with his group of fellow scouts, is kept at his foundation. In 1992, Agnès b. asked European photographers to write out, by hand, the story of their first photograph for her exhibition “Première photo” (“First Photo”) at the Galerie du Jour. Willy Ronis told his there. “There are no two first photographs, every photograph is unique, they all tell us something”, Luce Lebart sums up, having chosen to let that voice speak for itself rather than rewrite it as a wall text.

Luce Lebart also shows the first photographed Chinese atomic bomb test, but searched in vain for an equivalent French image. “I looked for the French one, I never found it;” she says, showing instead an indirect photograph: residents of the Sahara learning from the newspaper of the Gerboise Bleue test, and Malian students demonstrating two hundred kilometers from the site of the blast. The absence, here, says a great deal.

From that missing photograph to the ones splashed across a front page is a short step: the exhibition closes on the question of the front page. In 1980, Libération marked the death of Sartre, its co-founder, with its first-ever full-page photograph, a format the paper would later use for the obituaries of its own photographers, Sebastião Salgado and Martine Franck among them.

Two hundred years of firsts, then, and a conviction that runs through the whole show: invention, in photography as elsewhere, is never a solitary flash. It is made of trials, unclaimed patents, images that vanish before they are recognized. “Try again. Fail again. Fail better”, Beckett once wrote. Luce Lebart has made it a thread running through the whole exhibition, and Montpellier an open-air laboratory.

The exhibition “Premières fois / Premières photos” is on view at the Pavillon Populaire in Montpellier through November 1, 2026. Catalogue with texts by Luce Lebart, Jean-Paul Gandolfo and Amandine Gabriac, published by Spector Books, 2026.

items.title: Del Moral Among the Painters, Fifty Years of Intimacy
items.content:
Consider these boots first. Covered in white and black paint, planted on a floor just as spattered, they belong to Pierre Alechinsky, captured in Maussane in 1997. His face is nowhere to be seen, only what the gesture left on the leather: a map of a studio, in effect, more faithful than any portrait.

Jean Marie del Moral has photographed this kind of evidence for nearly 50 years. The son of Spanish Republican exiles, he began in photography at age 14, as an assistant in an aeronautics company’s photo department: studio work, artificial lighting, darkroom technique, the grammar of the craft before any notion of subject. At French newspaper L’Humanité, starting in 1973, he covered social affairs, then the Carnation Revolution, in Portugal, in 1974. The following year, settled in North America, he discovered at MoMA the Abstract Expressionists and the photographers who would always stay with him a little: Paul Strand, Walker Evans, Irving Penn, Manuel Alvarez Bravo.

Then came 1978, and Barcelona, where del Moral met Joan Miró for a story on Spanish intellectuals after Franco’s death. The encounter proved founding: ever since, he has never stopped photographing painters and sculptors at work, less for their finished pieces than for the moment just before, when nothing is yet fixed.

In Saumur, France the exhibition opens with seven large-format photographs of studio details, followed by a series of 46 portraits, then rooms devoted to emblematic studios. Pierre Soulages appears here, standing against a white wall in Sète in 1993, two brushes and a squeegee laid before him like surgical instruments. César appears too, in the marble of Pietrasanta, one hand resting on the shoulder of an antique statue, the other wrapped in a scarf. And Miquel Barceló, bent over a canvas laid flat on the floor of his Paris studio, surrounded by still-wet paintings, in 2006.

There are 56 artists in all, from Miró to Titus-Carmel, by way of Tàpies, Motherwell, Sam Francis, Schnabel, Tuymans, Katz, Mitchell, Zao Wou-Ki, Viallat, Morellet, Venet, Garouste, Raynaud, and Combas. 23 of them have already been shown at the Centre d’Art Contemporain Bouvet Ladubay over the past 30 years, and the exhibition closes a loop more than it opens a new one.

Del Moral published, in 2003 and again in 2004, Barceló, photographies Jean Marie del Moral (Barceló, Photographs by Jean Marie del Moral), successively with Thames and Hudson, Steidl, Actes Sud, and La Fabrica. But it is here, across the eight rooms of this art center founded in 1992 at the initiative of Patrice Monmousseau, that his work perhaps finds its truest setting, between tuffeau stone and the light of the Loire Valley.

As Juliette Monmousseau, general director of the Bouvet Ladubay estate, says, as it celebrates its 170th anniversary: “This exhibition is meant as a celebration of artistic creation through the eye of photographer Jean Marie del Moral.” What remains is the quiet evidence del Moral has been tracking for half a century: the work is made far from the spotlight, in dirty boots and silence.

“Ateliers et portraits d’artistes” (Studios and Portraits of Artists), by Jean Marie del Moral, is on view until October 30, 2026, at the Centre d’Art Contemporain Bouvet Ladubay in Saint-Hilaire-Saint-Florent, France.

items.title: The IRA and its shadow war, in the crosshairs
items.content:
IN IMAGES

The IRA and Its Shadow War, in the Crosshairs

Games of surveillance, false names and purloined documents make up the substance of a new book by Irish photographer Martin Cregg, titled The Plot.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Martin Cregg.

Photographer and educator, Martin Cregg coordinates the photography department at Pearse College of Further Education, in Dublin. With The Plot, he undertakes an artistic enquiry into the clandestine intelligence war waged between the IRA and British agents during the Irish War of Independence (1919-1921), within a “capital transformed into a theatre of espionage.”

Composed as a dialogue between contemporary photographs, historical documents and archival material, the book weaves the complex narrative of an Irish republican resistance determined to eliminate members of the Crown forces stationed in Dublin and to overthrow British occupation of Ireland.

Cregg’s research led him to photograph sites once devoted to military training, clandestine munitions factories and republican safe houses. Many of these locations were also the scenes of assassinations and failed ambush attempts. “The common street concealed the secret architecture of combat.”

This intelligence war was directed at the time by Michael Collins from a clandestine headquarters set up above a print shop on Crow Street, a stone’s throw from Dublin Castle. Ormonde Winter oversaw the “I Division” within the Castle, while David Neligan, an IRA mole, moved through its very heart. The organisation had its own squad of assassins, The Squad, within which “each man combined surveillance with lethal intent.”

Conceived as an object-book, in the image of the archives it summons, The Plot must first be “opened up.” Its sealed jacket veils its contents until the reader, blade in hand, slits open the front flap of the volume, following the dotted line provided for that purpose. Once “unsealed,” like a classified file, the volume reveals the weighty secrets that haunt its author’s inquiry, certain to captivate historians and enthusiasts of clandestine plots alike.

The Plot, by Martin Cregg, is published by Kehrer Verlag. Texts by Martin Cregg. Hardcover with open thread stitching and banderole. 288 pages. €48.

items.title: In the Dark, Benita Suchodrev Hunts Paradise
items.content:
IN IMAGES

In the Dark, Benita Suchodrev Hunts Paradise

Born in the Soviet Union and raised in suburban America before immersing herself in Berlin’s nightlife, Benita Suchodrev publishes Find Me Paradise with Kehrer Verlag. A book that recomposes twenty years of archives into dark, unsettling image pairs, in search of a light.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Benita Suchodrev.

The book grabs you from its opening pages. “An eye, a bird, a cherub, a sea monster,” writes author Simon Bainbridge, before noting that no logical thread unites them beyond a shared sense of dislocation. He goes on to describe one pairing: “A woman lies naked in an awkward pose, a broken doll atop a bare mattress.”

Benita Suchodrev owns this vertigo. Trained in art history and then English literature in the United States, she finds in Berlin a vantage point rather than a source of unease, fed by her immersion in its nightlife and underground art scene.

Her raw, unflinching images capture, in the publisher’s own words, “flashes of memory rooted in raw, unflinching realism…,” according to Kehrer Verlag. “Shifting between extremes, the surprising compositions cross the line between the beautiful and the grotesque,” the publisher adds.

Berlin’s images plunge us, as Bainbridge puts it, “head first into the vices of the city.” A man relieves himself beneath a huge extraction pipe, almost animal-like, paired with a photograph of a kettle whose spout and handle echo, almost comically, the scene opposite.

One of the oldest images in the book, a school of fish circling endlessly in an aquarium, sat in the photographer’s archive for twenty years before she rediscovered it during lockdown. Suchodrev sees in it a precise terror, that of “a promenade where people walk mechanically, like they’ve been switched on, and that horrifies me,” she says.

Her work echoes that of Anders Petersen and his Café Lehmitz, the essayist notes, sharing the same affinity for souls on the margins. Other, gentler images sharpen the unease by contrast: a fawn’s wide eyes facing the camera, a sleeping lamb, a column of light piercing the clouds, almost an Annunciation. “Paradise isn’t reached. It is searched for,” concludes Benita Suchodrev. In the depths of a Berlin club or in a child’s soft gaze, to each their own path.



Find Me Paradise by Benita Suchodrev is published by Kehrer Verlag. With texts by Simon Bainbridge and Benita Suchodrev. 400 pages, €50.
